digests.narrative:
His central claim this week is that the optical sell-off was unjustified and that demand visibility across the group is, in his words, stupidly high. He anchors it on three sets of earnings pointing the same way: Lumentum flagging unexpected demand and imbalance for ultra-high-power CW lasers with the ability to price ASPs up, MACOM and Applied Optoelectronics both pointing to extreme imbalance in lasers, TIAs and DSPs, and an Elazr general manager saying at an investor conference that the entire supply chain is out of stock and that shortages will run for years.

Applied Optoelectronics is where he does the most work and where his view moved. After the Rosenblatt summit he reported US-production premiums on 800G and 1.6T, several long-term agreements on the table that the company is declining so capacity is not blocked by one customer, being sold out at least through the second half of 2027, and 300-400mW lasers already in hand. He also modelled AOI closing on Lumentum's revenue by early 2028, calling the roughly $12B against $80B valuation gap interesting. Then on 21 August he turned: it is getting much harder to support the name when they keep dropping $500m and $600m ATMs, and the share structure is becoming shareholder-unfriendly even if the operating outlook is positive.

Sivers remains his favourite high-beta expression, on the argument that one small company supplies lasers into Jabil pluggables, POET and O-Net optical engines, Ayar optical I/O and GlobalFoundries photonic foundry work, with independent CW capacity arriving via Win Semi during a structural bottleneck. On POET itself he is openly uncomfortable, saying he has zero idea how the company was permitted to dilute so far, that it now holds roughly $830m of cash, and that he took only small positions.
keyPoints: Calls the optical de-rating absurd against demand visibility running through 2027 and beyond
AAOI: sold out through H2 2027, US-production ASP premiums, declining LTAs to keep capacity free
Turned on AAOI's financing on 21 Aug — repeated $500-600m ATMs called shareholder-unfriendly
SIVE framed as the high-beta long: lasers into JBL, POET/O-Net, Ayar and GFS at once
Openly critical of POET's dilution despite holding a small position
Lumentum confirmed CPO scale-up timelines, which he read as killing the delay rumours

digests.narrative:
He is firmly against the idea that the memory cycle is rolling over, and this week he kept arguing it from the NAND side. Phison's CEO expects 2027 capacity constraints to be more severe than 2026, on the reasoning that upstream suppliers need up to four years from plant construction to production, so with demand growing explosively and supply expansion limited the shortage runs for years. He has previously reported SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung sold out of 2027 DRAM and HBM capacity, with customers allocated only 60-70% of requested volumes.

Sandisk stays his cleanest expression of the argument. He reads the investor day as removing the cyclicality label outright — roughly 80% adjusted gross margins projected through 2030, around 75% operating margins, about 50% adjusted free cash flow margins, long-term agreements already covering two thirds of 2028 output, and minimum contracted revenue reaching $93B against a market capitalisation he cited near $239B. His question is how a company with revenue targets running four years out can be called cyclical.

He also keeps extending the pattern sideways. The MLCC work is the clearest example: Samsung lead times near 40 weeks, Murata moving 24 to 30 to 36 weeks, new capacity slipping from Q4 2026 into 2027, and his expectation that the same crowding-out squeeze hits consumer and general-purpose grades in late 2026 or early 2027 exactly as it did legacy DRAM. He read the US government urging Apple away from Chinese memory as a further tightening, noting that CXMT and YMTC are raising prices too, so the cheap-Chinese-supply argument does not hold.
keyPoints: Phison CEO: 2027 NAND constraints more severe than 2026; four-year lead times on new capacity
SNDK investor day read as disqualifying the cyclical label: ~80% GM through 2030, $93B contracted
SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung sold out of 2027 DRAM/HBM; customers allocated 60-70% of requests
MLCC lead times stretching to 36-40 weeks as the next crowding-out squeeze
US pressure on Apple over Chinese memory read as another tightening, with CXMT/YMTC also hiking

digests.narrative:
TSMC sits at the centre of his map — he describes it plainly as the centre of the AI buildout — and he uses it more as a source than as a trade, quoting it on memory and ABF substrate tightness over the coming years and naming it as the capacity provider behind the rest of the chain.

GlobalFoundries is the one he argues actively. He points to the US government taking a material stake and expects co-packaged optics to re-accelerate revenue, and earlier expressed surprise the stock stayed down given a direct government stake intended to advance CPO — reading it as good news that went unrewarded. It also appears in his Sivers case as the photonic foundry partner spanning NPO, pluggable and CPO architectures.

Samsung Foundry raising prices roughly 10-15% is noted as part of the same tightening, and he tracks Chinese capacity separately: YMTC pursuing an IPO next quarter after CXMT's successful listing, with the Chinese IPO market running hot from Unitree through to memory makers.
keyPoints: He calls TSMC the centre of the AI buildout and cites it on memory and ABF substrate tightness
GlobalFoundries: a material US government stake plus CPO should re-accelerate revenue
GF also appears as the photonic foundry partner in his Sivers thesis across NPO, pluggable and CPO
Samsung Foundry price hikes of roughly 10-15% read as further tightening
YMTC pursuing an IPO next quarter following CXMT, with the Chinese listing market running hot

digests.narrative:
He treats neocloud demand as settled and argues the read-through is enormous. CoreWeave's backlog above $104B, excluding more than $25B of new customer agreements added in early Q3, is his headline evidence, and he explicitly extends it to Nebius and IREN. Supermicro guiding $65-72B of revenue is cited alongside it as the same signal from the hardware side.

Nebius is the name he follows most closely. He called the last outlook insane again — $582.3M of revenue, up 454% year on year and 46% sequentially, at roughly 50% adjusted EBITDA margin in AI Cloud, with $8.04B of cash — while noting honestly that he had hoped for a guidance raise and only got a reiteration of $3.0-3.4B for 2026 and $7-9B exit ARR. He has also used the hyperscaler prints as a sarcastic argument against shorting it.

On the colocation side he flagged Riot's $9.1B twenty-year agreement, extendable to $16.1B, alongside AMD exercising its expansion option, and placed most of the basket's revenue inflection in the second half of 2027 — Riot's first 96MW targeted for December 2027. He grouped Nebius with the laser names as one of the places where 2027 demand visibility is unusually good.
keyPoints: CoreWeave's $104B+ backlog, excluding $25B+ added in early Q3, read across to NBIS and IREN
NBIS Q2: $582.3M revenue +454% Y/Y at ~50% adjusted EBITDA margin, $8.04B cash
Noted the guidance was reiterated, not raised — $3.0-3.4B revenue, $7-9B exit ARR
RIOT's $9.1B/20-year deal extendable to $16.1B, with AMD expanding separately
Colocation revenue inflections concentrated in H2 2027

digests.narrative:
Substrates are where he thinks the shortage is most visible and least priced. He posted the indium phosphide story as the clearest evidence yet: prices began rising in Q4 last year and the latest increase is the fourth consecutive one, expected to exceed 10%, while epitaxial wafer prices made from those substrates have already risen twice and are heading for a third increase. His favourite detail is a supplier saying that even if you have the money, you still may not be able to get the material.

He claims the call — he predicted the squeeze last year — and holds both AXT and IQE, saying his February IQE thesis was validated alongside AXT and that he remains long both. He notes the reporting is Taiwan-centric and names VPEC, Landmark and IET as beneficiaries, and treats MACOM's long-term epiwafer agreements and equity stake in IQE as a soft backstop that reads positive for IQE specifically.

On packaging he holds Amkor as a duration bet rather than a momentum one — bought on post-earnings weakness he found surprising given the Nvidia deal and a ten-year TSMC agreement, and explicitly described as more of a 2028 name with a separate 2027 ramp. Applied Materials raising advanced packaging growth guidance and extending customer discussions to 2030 supports the direction.
keyPoints: InP substrate prices up for a fourth consecutive quarter, the latest hike expected above 10%
Epitaxial wafer prices already raised twice, moving toward a third increase
Suppliers reportedly telling customers that money alone will not secure material
He is long both AXT and IQE and says he called the squeeze a year early
The cited reporting credits Taiwanese players VPEC, Landmark and IET as beneficiaries
Amkor held as a 2028 duration bet backstopped by Nvidia and a ten-year TSMC agreement

digests.narrative:
Marvell is the week's subject. Alphabet received options to buy $12.2B of the company across a broad range of TPU-related technologies — processors that run AI models, manage storage and move data across networks — which he suggests could translate into roughly $120B of revenue through 2033. He notes Marvell holds separate warrants with Amazon following the Celestial acquisition, and lists Marvell as one of the businesses NVIDIA has invested in directly, via Celestial.

He also uses the optical earnings to point at second-order beneficiaries. Applied Optoelectronics flagged DSP and TIA bottlenecks, which he read as a positive industry read-through for MaxLinear, then Semtech and MACOM. On Semtech specifically he declined to take a directional view, saying he has not modelled it recently, while arguing the architecture debate matters less for a supplier that benefits across many designs than for one focused on a single approach.

The broader framing he keeps returning to is that CPO is the next theme and that the remaining Western merchant suppliers of CW capacity — he lists AOI, MACOM, Broadcom, Sivers and Semtech — are where the scarcity value sits once NVIDIA has secured what it needs.
keyPoints: GOOGL granted options on $12.2B of MRVL stock across TPU technologies; ~$120B revenue to 2033
MRVL also holds separate AMZN warrants following the Celestial acquisition
AAOI's DSP and TIA bottleneck commentary read across to MXL, SMTC and MTSI
Declined a directional view on SMTC, citing no recent modelling
Names AVGO among the remaining Western merchant CW suppliers as CPO scales

digests.narrative:
This card changes shape this week: LPKF moves into the glass layer from materials, so the theme finally contains the name through which glass-substrate progress actually reaches the book. It is still only two tickers.

The news is a delay, and it is the analyst reporting a setback in his own theme, which is the kind of disclosure worth weighting heavily. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has delayed its semiconductor glass substrate investment on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, revising the start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back. For an equipment supplier this is worse than it is for a substrate maker: the tool order lands before the line runs, so a customer moving its start date right moves LPKF's revenue with it, and there is no partial credit. The share price is down about 12% on the month, which is the market reading the same thing.

Corning remains the other half of the card and has not moved: its glass-bridge case rests on 2028 fibre array unit TAM rather than anything shipping, and co-packaged optics delay reports weigh on that and the FAU case together. Conviction stays low. Glass is a 2028-2029 layer on current evidence, and the datapoint that would change this card is a disclosed tool order from a named substrate customer with a delivery year attached — not another timeline article.
keyPoints: LPK.DE re-categorised into glass from materials — the layer now holds the equipment exposure directly
Samsung Electro-Mechanics delays glass substrate start of operations to 2028; SKC also pushes back
Equipment leads the line, so a customer's slip moves LPKF's revenue event with it
LPK.DE is down about 12% on the month against a flat tape
GLW's glass-bridge case still rests on 2028 FAU TAM rather than current shipments
What would change the card: a disclosed LIDE order from a named customer with a delivery year

digests.narrative:
The Unitree listing is his anchor. It came public valued near $53.3B after rising 492% on debut, having been oversubscribed by retail more than 8,000 times, which he reads as proof that demand for pure-play humanoid exposure is far larger than assumed — and as a reason the leading US players should draw attention.

Agility via CCXI is his chosen expression and he is unusually explicit about the position: he bought between 0.25% and 0.75% of the float around announcement, at a $2.5B pre-money valuation, alongside SoftBank, NVIDIA, Amazon and Foxconn. His argument for it is commercial rather than technical — Agility is targeting commercialisation first, with robots already in Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouses, and he does not think a delivery or packaging robot needs to do backflips. He names Boston Dynamics as the closest peer on capability and notes Agility has been a laggard to its expected open price.

On Tesla he takes the form-factor side of the argument, quoting Musk that not all robots need to be humanoid but a general-purpose robot meant to replace human labour should fit the world humans already built, and expecting Optimus to converge there. His consistent caveat is that Optimus sits inside a company above $1T, so the exposure is diluted relative to a pure play.
keyPoints: Unitree listed near $53.3B, up 492% on debut, 8,000x oversubscribed by retail
Holds 0.25-0.75% of CCXI's float, entered at Agility's $2.5B pre-money
Case for Agility is commercialisation-first: Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouses, not backflips
Treats TSLA's Optimus as real but diluted inside a $1T+ company
Reads the Chinese humanoid listings as a catalyst for US pure-play attention

digests.narrative:
His organising idea is that NVIDIA telegraphs each theme roughly a year before the market prices it. His worked example is 2025: NVIDIA bought up EML and laser capacity while the market dismissed photonics as a bubble, and a year later Lumentum was up 678% and Applied Optoelectronics 475%. He extends the same logic forward — CPO is the next theme, NVIDIA secures the CW laser capacity, and the remaining Western merchant suppliers are where the value accrues.

He also tracks where NVIDIA has invested directly as a map of what it needs: Marvell via Celestial, Lumentum and Coherent in photonics, and Agility via CCXI in humanoids. On AOI he noted the company is declining long-term agreements specifically so its capacity is not blocked by one customer, pointing at NVIDIA as the implied party.

On AMD he says less analytically this week. It appears in his retrospective of ideas that played out and in the observation that AMD and NVIDIA disclosed billions in positions appearing in institutional filings. Earlier in the month he noted AMD exercising its option to expand the Riot arrangement, and placed most of the colocation basket's revenue inflection in the second half of 2027.
keyPoints: Core method: Jensen telegraphs the theme a year early and the market dismisses it each time
2025 EML/laser capacity buying cited as the proof case — LITE +678%, AAOI +475% a year later
Reads NVIDIA's direct investments (MRVL, LITE, COHR, CCXI) as a map of what it needs next
CPO named as the next theme, with NVIDIA expected to secure CW laser capacity
Colocation basket revenue inflections placed largely in H2 2027

digests.narrative:
He uses the hyperscalers as the demand proof rather than as positions. His summary of the last earnings round is that Amazon, Meta, Alphabet and Microsoft guided combined 2026 capex to roughly $720-745B, up from $695-725B previously, with Amazon at $220B, Google $195-205B, Meta $130-145B and Microsoft $175B. He raised Amazon's number himself after the quarter, noting it moved to $220B from $200B partly on higher memory costs, which he read as bullish for Micron and Samsung.

His sharper point is the gap between media framing and disclosure. Where the coverage said hyperscalers had overbuilt and were reselling excess compute, he pointed out that all four reported demand exceeding capacity. He quotes Jassy saying Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all 2026 demand and expects the same in 2027, with most incoming 2027 capacity already reserved and substantial 2028 capacity reserved too. He used the same material as a sarcastic template for how to research a short on Nebius — read the hyperscaler prints first, find record demand and backlog everywhere, then conclude.

The Marvell-Alphabet arrangement is the week's specific item: Marvell granting Alphabet options to buy $12.2B of the company across TPU-related technologies, which he suggests could translate into roughly $120B of revenue through 2033, with separate Amazon warrants following the Celestial acquisition.
keyPoints: 2026 combined capex guided to ~$720-745B, raised from $695-725B
Amazon's $220B guide raised on higher memory costs — read as confirmation for MU and Samsung
All four reported demand exceeding capacity, against media framing of overbuild
Jassy: most 2027 capacity already reserved, with substantial 2028 capacity reserved
MRVL granting GOOGL options on $12.2B of stock across TPU technologies

digests.narrative:
This layer exists because the desk built it, not because the feed produced it. Every thesis that touches power reaches it through a list rather than an argument. Bloom Energy is the only sustained name: it appears in a late-July recap for 166% year-on-year revenue growth with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance, and again in the note that grid power bottlenecks triggered a five-fold increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for its fuel cells. That financing line is the clearest power-constraint datapoint anywhere in the feed.

The second thread is a components one and sits mostly outside the US listed set: a shortage of high-power cylindrical cells for battery backup units, with Samsung SDI supplying Simplo, which assembles for Meta and Amazon, and both Panasonic and Samsung reported short. Vertiv, Eaton, EnerSys and BorgWarner are named only as adjacent read-throughs, and the analyst says plainly it is outside his domain.

GE Vernova and Constellation carry no analyst mentions at all, which is exactly the tiering caveat this layer was built to expose: grid interconnection, transformers and on-site generation are load-bearing for every gigawatt in the neocloud and hyperscaler digests, and the feed prices none of it. Conviction is low because the evidence is thin, not because the constraint is.
keyPoints: Desk-built layer: no thesis in the feed argues power directly, only in passing
BE is the only sustained name — 166% YoY revenue growth, raised 2026 guidance
Grid power bottlenecks drove a 5x increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for BE fuel cells
A BBU cylindrical-cell shortage runs through Samsung SDI, Panasonic and Murata, with no direct US listing
VRT, ETN and ENS appear only as adjacent read-throughs, explicitly outside the analyst's domain
GEV and CEG carry zero analyst mentions, so they cannot rise above radar however load-bearing they are
